title: Lesson 5: Connected Tools: Stitching the Apps You Already Use
description: Connected workflows: stitching the apps you already use into one flow, where one app's output feeds the next app's input via a handoff.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is a handed-off connection between two software applications that lets them work together without a human relaying data?
options: An application programming interface (API), the agreed set of rules or protocols that lets two apps communicate and exchange data
A saved prompt that only works inside a single chat window
A spreadsheet template you copy figures into by hand each week
A manual export followed by a re-import into the next app
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an API as the agreed way two pieces of software talk to each other, the set of rules or protocols that enables apps to communicate and exchange data, per IBM. The other options describe the manual relay work a connected workflow removes.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does a connected workflow need a review step at the end rather than shipping on its own?
options: Because an error in one link makes every later step wrong, and a confident-looking final output built on that mistake must be caught by a human before it matters
Because integrations cannot run without a person pressing a button to finish
Because the trigger will only fire when a human approves it first
Because downstream apps refuse to read output that was not human-reviewed
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that if step one is wrong, every step after it is wrong, so the output looks confident even when built on a mistake; the review stays at the end, keeping a human in the loop before the result matters, per the human-in-the-loop pattern.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which sign of a task makes it a strong candidate for a connected workflow?
options: It is frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk
It happens rarely and changes shape every time
It depends on information only you can supply and is irregular
It involves a high-risk decision that needs multiple human approvals
questions.explanation: The lesson repeats the Lesson 2 test for automatic: a connected workflow earns its keep when a task is frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk. Irregular, unpredictable, or high-judgment tasks are poor fits because automation wants a clear signal.
